seriesTitle: The Reckoner of the Thirteenth Hour
title: Emergency Reckoner

blocks.text: At nine o'clock an old man I had never met put a brass key and a thin printed book on the blotter at the Guild night desk. His hands were steady. His eyes were not.
'The Laws of Lull,' he said. 'You have three hours to read them. At midnight you Reckon for the Ninth Stair, or the Ninth Stair stops existing.'
There was a chair beside the desk. He looked at it and did not sit down.
Earlier that afternoon I had asked Cassius Orme why he had my job.

It had been his for eleven days. The card in the frame beside the Senior Night Auditor's door still said Sandor, because nobody had told the porter to change it, and Orme had slipped his own card in front of mine. He sat behind the desk with his hands folded on the blotter, the right over the left. He did not unfold them once while I spoke.

I said the committee had promised me the post in March, in writing. I said I had run the night desk for six years without a late Close or a missing figure. I said I did not want the post back. I wanted a reason.

'You were very thorough in your application, Miss Sandor,' he said. 'Admirably thorough. The committee weighed a great many things, and I am not at liberty to say which of them weighed most. I can tell you that it was not a judgement on your work, which everyone in this building respects, myself included. I hope you will go on doing it. The night desk needs you more than it will ever say.'
He smiled when he had finished. His hands stayed where they were.
I thanked him and went out. That was all he meant to give me, and I had known it before I knocked.

My father was a Guild clock-winder. There is something about him I am not ready to say. His name is in the Guild's records, and the committee had the records. I walked down the back stairs believing that someone on that committee had read my surname and remembered him, and that this was the reason. I believed it all afternoon, and I believed it at nine o'clock when the old man came.
I asked him for his name.
'Anselm Whitlow,' he said. 'I used to Reckon. I don't now. Pick up the key, Miss Sandor.'
'Why?'
'Because then it's in your hand,' he said, 'and what I tell you next goes to a keyholder. Wouldn't you rather I told you lawfully?'
I picked it up. It was heavier than a door key, plain brass, with a number stamped on the bow.

He told me about the Hour. At the first stroke of midnight from the Regulator, everyone inside the Escapement who was awake and holding their own key went into an hour the rest of the city never had, and came out at the same stroke. He said I had sat at this desk through it two thousand times and never noticed, because nobody does. He said there was a sport played in it, and a bank, and a currency, and debts.
I said I did not believe him.
He yawned, put the back of his hand to his mouth, and took it away as if he had done nothing. 'Then read the book,' he said. 'You'll want to know exactly what you don't believe.'

The rest he told me plainly. The Ninth Stair's Reckoner had walked out after the sixth matchday and said he wanted his nights back. The side was twelfth of twelve on four points. There were four of them, the fewest the Laws let play. Without a Reckoner tonight they forfeited, and the side at the bottom when the Turn ended was disbanded and its players' keys put away for a year.

'There's a thing in there called the Sponsor's Right,' he said. 'A retired Reckoner may lend his key to one emergency Reckoner for one match night. That's my key. You'd be the emergency. I stay out tonight. That's the price.'
'And afterwards?'
'The Bank has seven days to confirm you or refuse you. Confirm, and you get a key of your own. Refuse, and you'll have had one night. It can't be done twice for the same person.'
'Why me?'
'You're inside the wall at midnight every night and no one asks why,' he said. 'And you can add.'
'A great many people can add.'
'How many of them are sitting here?'
I said yes. I said yes because he had come to my desk and asked me to my face, and nobody had asked me for anything in years.
I wrote in the night book that I was inspecting the stair towers, which is one of my duties, and I went with him.

His flat was two streets inside the wall, up a flight above a locksmith's. He put a pot of tea at my elbow and the book in front of me and sat across the table with his hands round his own cup. I read the Laws of Lull through, every page, in order.

There were four clocks in the room. One on the mantel, one on the wall by the door, two on the dresser. At twenty-two minutes past nine the one by the door struck. At nine minutes to ten the mantel struck. Neither hour was an hour. The dresser clocks struck at ten past ten and at ten to eleven, and they did not agree with each other or with anything else.
'Why do your clocks disagree?' I asked.
'Why does anyone keep a clock?' he said. He looked at the one by the door and then at me. 'Read.'

I read. The ring of twelve plates and the Arbor in the middle. The Reckoner, who stands on the Arbor all match and cannot spend, and issues seconds by calling a name and a number until the player answers 'Held'. The Lull, in which a Sprinter spends and everyone not spending is frozen, and that included the Reckoner, in every Lull, on both sides. The sealed bank in the minute between rounds. The Tally. The Close. The Stall Book. I read the page on warm and cold seconds twice, because it was the only page that said how anything felt. The Reserve issues only cold seconds. A warm second has been drawn from someone's waiting within the last day.
At half past eleven I closed the book. He did not ask if I had understood it. He walked me to the Ninth Stair and stopped at the bottom step.
'I'll wait here,' he said. 'You won't be long. Nobody ever is.'

The landing at the top was cramped and every footstep came back twice. Twelve brass plates were set into the floor in a ring, numbered I to XII like a clock face, around a round raised platform with a rail. The Rate Board by the door showed each plate's posted rate in white paint. Three people were waiting by the rail.
The first was a young woman in a cut-down coat. She was talking before I reached the top step.
'You're the auditor. Whitlow's auditor.' She looked me up and down. 'Two coppers says she quits by round three. Who'll take it?'

'I'll take it,' said the second, a small woman sitting on the rail turning a screwdriver over and over in her fingers. 'Someone has to have faith.' She held out a hand to me without putting the screwdriver down. 'Tamsin Drewe. Winder. At last, someone to reckon with.'
The first woman groaned. 'Marguerite Lisle. Sprinter. Ignore her puns, everyone does.'
The third was a young man sitting on plate XII with his back against the wall and his eyes half shut. He lifted one hand.
'Bao Tran,' he said. 'Stiller. I'm the Keep.'
'Are you awake?' I asked.
'Mm.' He thought about it. 'I keep the plate. Keeping awake is harder.'
I called them Lisle, Drewe and Tran. I did not know them yet.

Chandler's Stair came up the stair at a quarter to twelve, five of them. Their Reckoner was a broad man with chalk on his cuffs who nodded to me once and went to his side of the Arbor. The Arbiter came last, a grey-haired woman with a Fob on a chain round her neck. She took both team sheets, read ours, and looked at me over it.
'Emergency Reckoner,' she said. 'Sponsor's Right?'
'Yes.'
She wrote something down and did not say anything else.
The first stroke came up through the soles of my shoes.
Nothing else changed. Through the landing window a man in the street below stood with one foot off the kerb and did not put it down.

I was afraid. I watched the Arbiter's hands while she set a glass jar on the shelf of the Arbor in front of me. The seal round its neck was dull brass. There was a small locked chamber inside the glass, for the bank. Three hundred seconds, the Stairwell Issue. She set the other jar in front of the Chandler's Reckoner, turned a slate and a stick of chalk the right way up for each of us, and stepped back.
'Round one,' she said.
The Token lay on plate I. It was a brass weight the size of a pocket watch. Plate I was one stride from plate XII, where Tran stood, and plate XII was the plate Chandler's had to reach.
Their Sprinter on plate I picked up the Token. He said, 'Spend, twelve.'

Nothing happened. Then the Token was lying on plate XII at Tran's feet. Their Sprinter was standing beside it with his hand open. Tran's hand was coming down from where the man's shoulder must have been. On the Tally board on the wall the figure under Chandler's Stair had gone from nought to twelve.
I had read that I would be frozen. I had not known it would be nothing at all. There was the word, and then there was the after.

'He came on my plate,' Tran told me at the end of the round, slowly, as if he were reading it off the inside of his eyelids. 'My Still was Set. It sprang when he said spend. Everything on the plate went slow but me. I put a hand on his shoulder. He put it down.'

The Token had been Spilled on XII. A Spilled Token never scores on the plate where it was Spilled. For the rest of the round their Sprinter stood on XII and looked at it, and every time he bent towards it Tran lifted one hand an inch. He did not bend far.
In the Bank minute I wrote nought on my slate, because I wanted to see his first. He wrote nought too. Equal banks score nothing.

Before round two Lisle bet Drewe a copper that the Arbiter would sneeze before round six. She bet their Keep, across the ring, that he would drop the Token if he ever got it. She had bet on me before she knew my name. I watched her do it and made up my mind. A woman who bets on everything spends the same way. I decided to keep her short.
'Lisle, fifteen,' I said.
She looked at me. 'Fifteen?'
'Held,' she said, after a moment.
The Token started on plate II. Our target was plate VI, four strides away. She picked it up and said, 'Spend, fifteen.'
Then she was standing on plate IV with the Token on the floor at her feet and a Chandler's player's hand just leaving her arm. The Tally said we had spent fifteen.
'Dry on four,' she said, when the round was over and she had walked back to the rail. Her face was red. 'Two plates short. Two. You sent me to market with a ha'penny, auditor.'
Chandler's wrote seven in the Bank minute. I wrote nought again. One-nil.
Tran came to the rail while the Arbiter was wiping the slates. He spoke so quietly that I had to lean over.
'She doesn't waste them,' he said. 'Never has. Not one second in a Lull. She spends what the run needs and brings the rest home.'
'She bets on everything.'
'Mm. With coppers.' He looked at Lisle. 'Not with seconds.'
He had seen every Lull he had ever been sprung in. I had seen none. I had judged her on what she did with her mouth and not on what she did with her hands, and it had cost us a run.
I said it to her. 'I was wrong about you. I gave you fifteen because I thought you'd waste sixty. You'll have a full issue from now on.'
Lisle stared at me. 'Two coppers says you don't.'
'I don't bet.'
'Course you don't,' she said, but she was nearly smiling.
'Lisle, sixty,' I said in round three.
'Held.'

The Token started on III. She said, 'Spend,' and a number, and then it was on plate VI and she was taking her hand away from it, and the Arbiter said, 'Ninth Stair, two.' Afterwards she told me she had crossed four and five with their Stiller on five sprung and crawling, and had brought most of the sixty home. The Tally agreed with her to the second.
At the end of round three Lisle paid Drewe two coppers, because I had not quit.
'Thank you,' Drewe said, and put them in her waistcoat. 'Every little cog.'

The middle of the match went the way the middle of most things goes. Chandler's scored in round four on a far start with two spenders, and Tran said afterwards that he had touched the wrong one. They scored again in round eight. Lisle got the Token as far as their Stillers every round and no farther, and twice she came back to the rail with her mouth shut tight and said nothing at all.

I watched the Chandler's Reckoner. He wrote his slates quickly, with his left hand cupped round them, and he did not look at me while he wrote. When his side were level or behind, he wrote whatever he liked: nought, seven, nine, thirteen. When they were ahead going into a Bank minute, his hand made the same two strokes. Ten. Four times that night they went into a Bank minute ahead, and four times he wrote ten.
I beat him all four times, with twelve, fifteen, fourteen and twelve. I did not once write eleven. I did not want him to see that I had seen it.
Going into round twelve, Chandler's had seven points and we had six.

The Token started on plate XII, our own Hour plate, six strides from theirs either way round. The Tally said we had spent a hundred and ninety-three and banked sixty-six. Three hundred less both was forty-one. That was every second I had left.

If I gave Lisle all forty-one, she might get a far start home, and she might not. If she did not, I would have nothing for the slate, and he would write ten, and we would lose by two. If I kept back the cheapest bid that beat his habit, I could give her the rest.
'Lisle, thirty,' I said.
'Held.'

She got as far as plate III. Their Stiller there was sprung when she arrived, and their man on III had his hand on her arm before her count ran out. The Token lay dead on III when the four minutes ended. Chandler's never lifted it.
'Bank,' said the Arbiter.
The landing was very quiet. Drewe had stopped turning the screwdriver. Lisle was standing on plate IV with both hands in her coat pockets.
I was afraid. I watched his hand. He cupped it round the slate. His wrist moved twice and stopped.
I wrote eleven and turned my slate face down.
The Arbiter took both slates and turned them over together.
'Chandler's Stair, ten,' she said. 'Ninth Stair, eleven. Bank to the Ninth Stair. Seven points all.'
Nobody said anything for a moment. Then Drewe said, 'Oh,' and Tran said, 'Mm,' very softly, and the Chandler's Reckoner looked at my slate for a long time and then at me.
A draw. One point. Five on the table.
Lisle came to the rail and looked at me as if I had taken a coin out of her ear.
'How did you do that?'
'It was his slates,' I said. 'He writes ten when they're ahead. It wasn't a trick.'
'Two coppers says it was a trick,' she said, and went to tell Tran.

The stroke came at the end of the Hour exactly as it had at the beginning. Through the window the man in the street put his foot down on the cobbles and walked on. At the bottom of the Ninth Stair, Whitlow had his hand halfway to his mouth, at the end of the same yawn.
He looked at my face and then at the jar under my arm.
'A fat jar?' he asked.
'I don't know yet,' I said.

The Close was in the porter's lodge at the foot of the stair, where the Bank had a clerk at a folding table with a ledger, a declaration form, a brass scale and a pen. The clerk was young and had ink on his second finger. He pushed the scale towards me without looking up.

The Close was work, and I did it the way I did my work. The Issue was three hundred. The Tally at the end of round twelve said we had spent two hundred and twenty-three and banked seventy-seven. Three hundred less two hundred and twenty-three was seventy-seven. The jar should have held its bank and not a second more.
I set it on the scale. The needle went past seventy-seven and stopped at a hundred and twenty-four.
Forty-seven over.

I took the jar off the scale and held it in both hands, with no gloves, and stood still with it. I paid attention. The glass was warm. Not warm from my arm, or the lodge stove, which was out. Warm from inside, like a cup someone has just put down.
The Stall Book page lay beside the form. I left it blank. I did not know where any of them would be next week.
The clerk had turned the declaration round to face me and was holding out the pen.

By the printed Laws the Reserve issues only cold seconds, so forty-seven warm ones had come into our jar from outside it within the last day, and I had a few minutes to sign a Close declaration that, if I wrote down what I had weighed, could cost the Ninth Stair the draw we had just won.
